claim: NKG2D is engaged in vivo by RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in healthy WT mice the NK activating receptor NKG2D is engaged in vivo by one of its ligands, RAE-1ε, which is expressed constitutively by lymph node endothelial cells and highly induced on tumor-associated endothelium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing NKG2D upregulation after RAE-1ε blockade and elevated NKG2D in RAE-1-KO mice.

claim: RAE-1ε is expressed constitutively by lymph node endothelial cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in healthy WT mice the NK activating receptor NKG2D is engaged in vivo by one of its ligands, RAE-1ε, which is expressed constitutively by lymph node endothelial cells and highly induced on tumor-associated endothelium.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing RAE-1ε expression on lymph node endothelial cells.

claim: RAE-1ε is highly induced on tumor-associated endothelium.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in healthy WT mice the NK activating receptor NKG2D is engaged in vivo by one of its ligands, RAE-1ε, which is expressed constitutively by lymph node endothelial cells and highly induced on tumor-associated endothelium.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing elevated RAE-1ε on tumor-associated endothelial cells compared to lymph node endothelial cells.

claim: NKG2D-RAE-1ε interaction causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
source: This interaction causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface and transmits an NK-intrinsic signal that desensitizes NK cell responses globally to acute stimulation, resulting in impaired NK antitumor responses in vivo.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased NKG2D surface levels after RAE-1ε blockade and in RAE-1-KO mice.

claim: NKG2D-RAE-1ε interaction transmits an NK-intrinsic signal that desensitizes NK cell responses globally to acute stimulation.
source: This interaction causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface and transmits an NK-intrinsic signal that desensitizes NK cell responses globally to acute stimulation, resulting in impaired NK antitumor responses in vivo.
evidence: Supported by functional assays showing hyper-responsiveness of NK cells from RAE-1-KO and NKG2D-KO mice, and bone marrow chimera experiments demonstrating cell-intrinsic effects.

claim: NKG2D-RAE-1ε interaction results in impaired NK antitumor responses in vivo.
source: This interaction causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface and transmits an NK-intrinsic signal that desensitizes NK cell responses globally to acute stimulation, resulting in impaired NK antitumor responses in vivo.
evidence: Supported by tumor challenge experiments showing enhanced tumor control in NKG2D-KO and RAE-1-KO mice.

claim: NK cells respond to infected or transformed cells by releasing cytotoxic granules and anti-tumor cytokines such as interferon-γ (IFNγ).
source: NK cells respond to infected or transformed cells by releasing cytotoxic granules and anti-tumor cytokines such as interferon-γ (IFNγ) (Vivier et al., 2008; Marcus et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cells recognize unhealthy cells using an array of cell surface receptors.
source: NK cells recognize unhealthy cells using an array of cell surface receptors (Vivier et al., 2011; Marcus et al., 2014; Moretta et al., 2014; Morvan and Lanier, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumors are often recognized and killed by NK cells in vitro and in vivo because cancer cells tend to upregulate ligands for activating receptors and downregulate ligands for inhibitory receptors.
source: Tumors are often recognized and killed by NK cells in vitro and in vivo because cancer cells tend to upregulate ligands for activating receptors and downregulate ligands for inhibitory receptors (Waldhauer and Steinle, 2008; Marcus et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The responsiveness of NK cells to a given stimulus is dynamically tuned by the steady-state receptor-ligand interactions experienced by the NK cells.
source: The responsiveness of NK cells to a given stimulus is dynamically tuned by the steady-state receptor-ligand interactions experienced by the NK cells (Joncker and Raulet, 2008; Brodin et al., 2009; Joncker et al., 2009; Joncker et al., 2010; Shifrin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increases in steady-state stimulation cause NK cells to compensate by adopting a less responsive state.
source: Increases in steady-state stimulation cause NK cells to compensate by adopting a less responsive state (Joncker et al., 2010; Kadri et al., 2016) – a process that will be referred to here as 'desensitization' – whereas NK cells receiving lower steady-state levels of stimulation exhibit a state of heightened responsiveness to acute activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cells receiving lower steady-state levels of stimulation exhibit a state of heightened responsiveness to acute activation.
source: Increases in steady-state stimulation cause NK cells to compensate by adopting a less responsive state (Joncker et al., 2010; Kadri et al., 2016) – a process that will be referred to here as 'desensitization' – whereas NK cells receiving lower steady-state levels of stimulation exhibit a state of heightened responsiveness to acute activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice lacking MHC I molecules or inhibitory Ly49 receptors show dramatically weaker NK responses to a wide variety of acute stimulatory signals in vitro and in vivo.
source: Mice lacking MHC I molecules or inhibitory Ly49 receptors show dramatically weaker NK responses to a wide variety of acute stimulatory signals in vitro and in vivo (Liao et al., 1991; Fernandez et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2005; Anfossi et al., 2006; Brodin et al., 2009; Joncker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mature NK cells can alter their responsiveness upon encountering a new MHC I environment.
source: Desensitization may prevent NK cells from effecting autoreactivity and enable them to adjust to different tissue milieus, and mature NK cells can alter their responsiveness upon encountering a new MHC I environment (Joncker and Raulet, 2008; Elliott et al., 2010; Joncker et al., 2010; Narni-Mancinelli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cells in WT mice become desensitized when they infiltrate MHC I-deficient tumors but not when they infiltrate matched MHC-I-positive tumors.
source: These dynamics are relevant for antitumor responses, as NK cells in WT mice become desensitized when they infiltrate MHC I-deficient tumors but not when they infiltrate matched MHC-I-positive tumors (Ardolino et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Humans receiving HLA-mismatched bone marrow show altered NK responses that match the trends described in mice.
source: Similarly, humans receiving HLA-mismatched bone marrow show altered NK responses that match the trends described in mice (Boudreau et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of NK activating ligands causes NK desensitization.
source: Indeed, transgenic overexpression of NK activating ligands causes NK desensitization (Oppenheim et al., 2005; Wiemann et al., 2005; Sun and Lanier, 2008; Tripathy et al., 2008), but the endogenous receptor-ligand systems that transmit these activating signals to NK cells in healthy WT animals remain incompletely defined.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The endogenous receptor-ligand systems that transmit activating signals to NK cells in healthy WT animals remain incompletely defined.
source: Indeed, transgenic overexpression of NK activating ligands causes NK desensitization (Oppenheim et al., 2005; Wiemann et al., 2005; Sun and Lanier, 2008; Tripathy et al., 2008), but the endogenous receptor-ligand systems that transmit these activating signals to NK cells in healthy WT animals remain incompletely defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In humans, activating KIR appear to be one endogenous signal involved in steady-state NK cell tuning.
source: In humans, activating KIR appear to be one such endogenous signal involved in steady-state NK cell tuning (Fauriat et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKp46-KO animals showed heightened NK responses to stimulation in one report.
source: In mice, the activating receptor NKp46 may contribute to NK desensitization because NKp46-KO animals showed heightened NK responses to stimulation in one report (Narni-Mancinelli et al., 2012), although not in another (Sheppard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKp46-KO animals did not show heightened NK responses to stimulation in another report.
source: In mice, the activating receptor NKp46 may contribute to NK desensitization because NKp46-KO animals showed heightened NK responses to stimulation in one report (Narni-Mancinelli et al., 2012), although not in another (Sheppard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SLAM receptors are reported to regulate NK responsiveness in some contexts.
source: SLAM receptors are also reported to regulate NK responsiveness in some contexts (Chen et al., 2016) (Veillette, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MHC-I-deficient nonhematopoietic cells may play a larger role than MHC-I-deficient hematopoietic cells in desensitizing NK cells.
source: A recent study using β2M-KO bone marrow chimeras suggested that MHC-I-deficient nonhematopoietic cells may play a larger role than MHC-I-deficient hematopoietic cells in desensitizing NK cells, although both may participate (Shifrin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Different studies have implicated HLA molecules on hematopoietic cells as being critical for tuning in humans.
source: In humans, different studies have implicated HLA molecules on hematopoietic cells (Haas et al., 2011) and nonhematopoietic cells (Cooley et al., 2011) as being critical for tuning.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Different studies have implicated HLA molecules on nonhematopoietic cells as being critical for tuning in humans.
source: In humans, different studies have implicated HLA molecules on hematopoietic cells (Haas et al., 2011) and nonhematopoietic cells (Cooley et al., 2011) as being critical for tuning.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D is a C-type lectin-like activating receptor expressed by all NK cells and subsets of T cells.
source: NKG2D is a C-type lectin-like activating receptor expressed by all NK cells and subsets of T cells (Raulet, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D binds a diverse array of MHC-like proteins.
source: NKG2D binds a diverse array of MHC-like proteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NKG2D.

claim: In mice, NKG2D ligands include the RAE-1 family (with α, β, γ, δ, and ε isoforms), the H60 family (a, b, c), and MULT1.
source: In mice, these include the RAE-1 family (with α, β, γ, δ, and ε isoforms), the H60 family (a, b, c), and MULT1.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mouse NKG2D ligands.

claim: Human NKG2D ligands include the ULBP family (with isoforms 1–6) and the MICA and MICB proteins.
source: Human NKG2D ligands include the ULBP family (with isoforms 1–6) and the MICA and MICB proteins (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Acute NKG2D engagement transmits powerful activating signals through the adaptor molecules DAP10 and DAP12 to drive cytotoxicity and cytokine production.
source: Acute NKG2D engagement transmits powerful activating signals through the adaptor molecules DAP10 and DAP12 to drive cytotoxicity and cytokine production (Raulet, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D ligands are thought to be absent from most healthy cells but can be induced consequent to DNA damage, oncogene signaling, and other stresses associated with cancer and infection.
source: NKG2D ligands are thought to be absent from most healthy cells but can be induced consequent to DNA damage, oncogene signaling, and other stresses associated with cancer and infection (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Many tumor cells express NKG2D ligands.
source: Many tumor cells express NKG2D ligands.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: In tumor transplant and spontaneous cancer models, expression of NKG2D ligand(s) on tumor cells triggers NK activation and protects the host from cancer.
source: In tumor transplant and spontaneous cancer models, expression of NKG2D ligand(s) on tumor cells triggers NK activation and protects the host from cancer (Diefenbach et al., 2001; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cells in NKG2D-KO mice are hyper-responsive to stimulation when triggered through other activating receptors.
source: Interestingly, several recent studies have shown that NK cells in NKG2D-KO mice are hyper-responsive to stimulation when triggered through other activating receptors (Zafirova et al., 2009; Sheppard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumor cells engineered to secrete soluble monomeric NKG2D ligands increase the responsiveness of tumor-infiltrating NK cells and enhance tumor rejection.
source: Furthermore, tumor cells engineered to secrete soluble monomeric NKG2D ligands – which block but do not activate NKG2D – increase the responsiveness of tumor-infiltrating NK cells and enhance tumor rejection (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D may contribute to NK desensitization at steady state or in tumors.
source: These data suggest that NKG2D may contribute to NK desensitization at steady state or in tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies showing NK hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice and effects of soluble NKG2D ligands.

claim: In vivo blockade of RAE-1ε substantially increased NKG2D surface levels on NK cells in blood.
source: In vivo blockade of RAE-1ε, but not RAE-1δ or MULT1, substantially increased NKG2D surface levels on NK cells in blood (Figure 1A), lymph nodes, and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In vivo blockade of RAE-1δ or MULT1 did not substantially increase NKG2D surface levels on NK cells in blood.
source: In vivo blockade of RAE-1ε, but not RAE-1δ or MULT1, substantially increased NKG2D surface levels on NK cells in blood (Figure 1A), lymph nodes, and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NKG2D elevation after RAE-1ε blockade occurred as early as 12 hr after antibody injection.
source: NKG2D elevation after RAE-1ε blockade occurred as early as 12 hr after antibody injection (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RAE-1-KO mice contain frameshift mutations (induced by CRISPR/Cas9) in the genes for both RAE-1ε and RAE-1δ.
source: We subsequently analyzed NKG2D surface levels in RAE-1-KO mice, which contain frameshift mutations (induced by CRISPR/Cas9) in the genes for both RAE-1ε and RAE-1δ (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature describing the generation of these mice.

claim: NK cells in RAE-1-KO mice showed substantially higher cell surface NKG2D levels than WT controls in blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and peritoneal wash.
source: In healthy, unmanipulated animals, NK cells in RAE-1-KO mice showed substantially higher cell surface NKG2D levels than WT controls in all compartments tested, including blood, spleen, lymph nodes, and peritoneal wash (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NK cells in bone marrow and liver showed elevated NKG2D levels in RAE-1-KO mice.
source: NK cells in bone marrow and liver also showed elevated NKG2D levels in RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mRNA levels for Klrk1 (the gene for NKG2D) were identical in NK cells from WT and RAE-1-KO mice.
source: mRNA levels for Klrk1 (the gene for NKG2D) were identical in NK cells from WT and RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1D), consistent with the conclusion that host RAE-1ε causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Host RAE-1ε causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
source: mRNA levels for Klrk1 (the gene for NKG2D) were identical in NK cells from WT and RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1D), consistent with the conclusion that host RAE-1ε causes internalization of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NKG2D mRNA levels are identical but surface protein levels differ between WT and RAE-1-KO mice.

claim: Blocking RAE-1ε in WT mice increased NKG2D to levels comparable to RAE-1-KO mice at steady state.
source: Blocking RAE-1ε in WT mice increased NKG2D to levels comparable to RAE-1-KO mice at steady state, whereas anti-RAE-1ε had no effect on NKG2D levels in RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Anti-RAE-1ε had no effect on NKG2D levels in RAE-1-KO mice.
source: Blocking RAE-1ε in WT mice increased NKG2D to levels comparable to RAE-1-KO mice at steady state, whereas anti-RAE-1ε had no effect on NKG2D levels in RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Blockade of RAE-1ε in combination with RAE-1δ in WT mice showed no additional effect on NKG2D levels compared with blocking RAE-1ε alone.
source: Furthermore, blockade of RAE-1ε in combination with RAE-1δ in WT mice showed no additional effect on NKG2D levels compared with blocking RAE-1ε alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: When splenocytes were transferred from WT to RAE-1-KO mice, NKG2D levels on the transferred NK cells increased to match the RAE-1-KO mice.
source: When splenocytes were transferred from WT to RAE-1-KO mice, NKG2D levels on the transferred NK cells increased to match the RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from splenocyte transfer experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NKG2D surface levels were reduced on NK cells transferred from RAE-1-KO into WT mice.
source: Reciprocally, NKG2D surface levels were reduced on NK cells transferred from RAE-1-KO into WT mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from splenocyte transfer experiments.

claim: In healthy WT mice a subset of cells express RAE-1ε, which engages and downregulates NKG2D at steady state from the surface of NK cells.
source: Cumulatively, these data demonstrated that in healthy WT mice a subset of cells express RAE-1ε, which engages and downregulates NKG2D at steady state from the surface of NK cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Splenic NK cell numbers were similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice.
source: Splenic NK cell numbers and expression of CD11b and CD27 – cell surface markers associated with NK maturation (Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006) – were similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of CD11b and CD27 were similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice.
source: Splenic NK cell numbers and expression of CD11b and CD27 – cell surface markers associated with NK maturation (Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006) – were similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD11b and CD27 are cell surface markers associated with NK maturation.
source: Splenic NK cell numbers and expression of CD11b and CD27 – cell surface markers associated with NK maturation (Hayakawa and Smyth, 2006) – were similar in WT and RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A significantly greater percentage of NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice responded to NKp46 stimulation compared with WT NK cells.
source: As is typical with this assay, stimulation through the activating receptor NKp46 triggered robust NK cell degranulation and IFNγ production from WT splenic NK cells, and a significantly greater percentage of NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice responded to stimulation compared with WT NK cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice showed elevated responses when stimulated with platebound antibodies that ligate NK1.1 or NKG2D.
source: NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice also showed elevated responses when stimulated with platebound antibodies that ligate a distinct activating receptor, NK1.1, or that ligate NKG2D itself (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Splenic NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice exhibit a hyper-responsive phenotype upon acute stimulation through a variety of activating receptors.
source: These data indicated that splenic NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice exhibit a hyper-responsive phenotype upon acute stimulation through a variety of activating receptors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing elevated responses to multiple stimuli.

claim: Peritoneal NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice showed markedly greater responses compared with their WT counterparts when stimulated through NKp46, NK1.1 or NKG2D.
source: Interestingly, peritoneal NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice showed markedly greater responses compared with their WT counterparts when stimulated through NKp46, NK1.1 or NKG2D (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Blockade of RAE-1ε caused a substantial increase in NK responses to stimulation through all receptors tested.
source: Similar to the RAE-1-KO mice, blockade of RAE-1ε caused a substantial increase in NK responses to stimulation through all receptors tested (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays after antibody blockade shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increased responses after RAE-1ε blockade could be seen as early as 48 hr after antibody administration.
source: The increased responses could be seen as early as 48 hr after antibody administration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from time course experiments.

claim: NKG2D-KO effectors were significantly less efficient at killing YAC-1 cells.
source: NKG2D-KO effectors were significantly less efficient at killing YAC-1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), consistent with published reports showing that NKG2D-mediated recognition is required for efficient YAC-1 killing (Jamieson et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2D-mediated recognition is required for efficient YAC-1 killing.
source: NKG2D-KO effectors were significantly less efficient at killing YAC-1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), consistent with published reports showing that NKG2D-mediated recognition is required for efficient YAC-1 killing (Jamieson et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RAE-1-KO mice showed markedly enhanced NK killing of YAC-1 cells.
source: In contrast, RAE-1-KO mice showed markedly enhanced NK killing of YAC-1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Endogenous, steady-state RAE-1ε expression desensitizes NK responses to activation through multiple activating receptors and YAC-1 cells in vitro.
source: Together, these data suggested that endogenous, steady-state RAE-1ε expression desensitizes NK responses to activation through multiple activating receptors and YAC-1 cells in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing hyper-responsiveness in RAE-1-KO mice.

claim: NKG2D-KO NK cells from spleen and peritoneal wash showed increased responses to stimulation compared with WT controls when stimulated through NKp46 and NK1.1.
source: Indeed, NKG2D-KO NK cells from spleen and peritoneal wash showed increased responses to stimulation compared with WT controls when stimulated through NKp46 and NK1.1 (Figure 3A and B), as has also been previously reported (Zafirova et al., 2009; Sheppard et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 3A and B, and citations to published literature.

claim: When stimulated with platebound antibody ligating NKG2D, NK cells from RAE-1-KO showed elevated responses, whereas NKG2D-KO NK cells failed to respond.
source: When stimulated with platebound antibody ligating NKG2D, NK cells from RAE-1-KO showed elevated responses, whereas NKG2D-KO NK cells failed to respond, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Stimulation through NKp46 resulted in elevated responses from both the RAE-1-KO and NKG2D-KO cohorts.
source: In contrast, stimulation through NKp46 resulted in elevated responses from both the RAE-1-KO and NKG2D-KO cohorts (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NKG2D-KO NK cells were consistently even more responsive than the NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice.
source: Interestingly, NKG2D-KO NK cells were consistently even more responsive than the NK cells from RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In addition to RAE-1ε, other ligands may participate in NKG2D-mediated desensitization, or NKG2D may regulate NK responses partly through a ligand-independent mechanism.
source: These data suggested that, in addition to RAE-1ε, other ligands may participate in NKG2D-mediated desensitization, or NKG2D may regulate NK responses partly through a ligand-independent mechanism in addition to the RAE-1ε-dependent mechanism documented herein.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NKG2D-KO NK cells are more responsive than RAE-1-KO NK cells.

claim: NKG2D-KO NK cells were hyper-responsive compared with WT NK cells in mixed chimeric mice containing both WT and NKG2D-KO NK cells.
source: Interestingly, NK cells from the mixed chimeras recapitulated these responses, as NKG2D-KO NK cells were hyper-responsive compared with WT NK cells in the same animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NKG2D desensitizes NK responses in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: These data demonstrated that NKG2D desensitizes NK responses in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the bone marrow chimera experiments showing that WT and NKG2D-KO NK cells behave differently in the same animal.

claim: Chimeric mice in which RAE-1ε was present only in hematopoietic cells (WT → KO) showed high NKG2D levels comparable to KO → KO chimeras.
source: Chimeric mice in which RAE-1ε was present only in hematopoietic cells (WT → KO) showed high NKG2D levels comparable to KO → KO chimeras, indicating that hematopoietic RAE-1ε does not play a major role in engaging NKG2D, although there was a reproducibly small effect in most experiments that failed to reach significance.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: Hematopoietic RAE-1ε does not play a major role in engaging NKG2D.
source: Chimeric mice in which RAE-1ε was present only in hematopoietic cells (WT → KO) showed high NKG2D levels comparable to KO → KO chimeras, indicating that hematopoietic RAE-1ε does not play a major role in engaging NKG2D, although there was a reproducibly small effect in most experiments that failed to reach significance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WT → KO chimeras have high NKG2D levels similar to KO → KO chimeras.

claim: Mice with RAE-1ε expression restricted to nonhematopoietic cells (KO → WT) completely recapitulated the low NKG2D levels seen in WT → WT animals.
source: In contrast, mice with RAE-1ε expression restricted to nonhematopoietic cells (KO → WT) completely recapitulated the low NKG2D levels seen in WT → WT animals (Figure 4A) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nonhematopoietic RAE-1 played a dominant role in the desensitization of NK responses.
source: When we analyzed the functional responses of NK cells in these chimeras, a similar pattern emerged, with nonhematopoietic RAE-1 playing a dominant role in the desensitization of NK responses, although hematopoietic RAE-1 did show some effect (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays in bone marrow chimeras shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hematopoietic RAE-1 showed some effect in the desensitization of NK responses.
source: When we analyzed the functional responses of NK cells in these chimeras, a similar pattern emerged, with nonhematopoietic RAE-1 playing a dominant role in the desensitization of NK responses, although hematopoietic RAE-1 did show some effect (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from NK responsiveness assays in bone marrow chimeras shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant source of RAE-1ε that engages NKG2D and regulates NK cell responsiveness.
source: These data suggested that nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant source of RAE-1ε that engages NKG2D and regulates NK cell responsiveness.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: Blood endothelial cells (BECs) and lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) in inguinal lymph nodes from naive B6 mice express substantial RAE-1ε.
source: We isolated inguinal lymph nodes from naive B6 mice and used flow cytometry to analyze RAE-1ε on these four populations. Whereas DN cells and FRCs showed little to no RAE-1ε, we found substantial RAE-1ε expression on BECs and LECs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DN cells and FRCs in inguinal lymph nodes showed little to no RAE-1ε.
source: We isolated inguinal lymph nodes from naive B6 mice and used flow cytometry to analyze RAE-1ε on these four populations. Whereas DN cells and FRCs showed little to no RAE-1ε, we found substantial RAE-1ε expression on BECs and LECs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RAE-1ε staining on lymph node endothelial cells was not due to promiscuous binding of the RAE-1ε antibody.
source: This was not due to promiscuous binding of the RAE-1ε antibody, because the staining completely disappeared in RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing absence of staining in RAE-1-KO mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Splenic CD31-hi endothelial cells express low amounts of RAE-1ε.
source: Splenic CD31-hi endothelial cells did express low amounts of RAE-1ε, but endothelial cells in the lung, liver, and heart showed little to no RAE-1ε (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Endothelial cells in the lung, liver, and heart showed little to no RAE-1ε.
source: Splenic CD31-hi endothelial cells did express low amounts of RAE-1ε, but endothelial cells in the lung, liver, and heart showed little to no RAE-1ε (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: RAE-1ε expression was substantially higher on HEV cells than the average expression on non-HEV BECs.
source: Interestingly, RAE-1ε expression was substantially higher on HEV cells than the average expression on non-HEV BECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant compartment responsible for steady state RAE-1ε-mediated NKG2D engagement and NK desensitization.
source: In summary, these experiments showed that nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant compartment responsible for steady state RAE-1ε-mediated NKG2D engagement and NK desensitization, and our analysis of cellular RAE-1ε expression implicate endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid tissue as the relevant cellular source for RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the bone marrow chimera and flow cytometry experiments.

claim: Endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid tissue are the relevant cellular source for RAE-1ε.
source: In summary, these experiments showed that nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant compartment responsible for steady state RAE-1ε-mediated NKG2D engagement and NK desensitization, and our analysis of cellular RAE-1ε expression implicate endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid tissue as the relevant cellular source for RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that endothelial cells in lymph nodes express RAE-1ε and nonhematopoietic cells are the dominant source.

claim: NK cells, trafficking in and out of lymphoid tissue during homeostatic circulation, are continuously engaged and desensitized by RAE-1ε expressed on endothelial cells.
source: These findings suggest a model in which NK cells, trafficking in and out of lymphoid tissue during homeostatic circulation, are continuously engaged and desensitized by RAE-1ε expressed on endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: B16 is a classic syngeneic tumor model that is sensitive to NK killing but lacks NKG2D ligand expression.
source: To study the effects of endogenous RAE-1ε in tumor microenvironments, we used the B16-BL6 (hereafter called B16) model of melanoma, a classic syngeneic tumor model that is sensitive to NK killing but lacks NKG2D ligand expression (Lakshmikanth et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking RAE-1ε but not RAE-1δ caused dramatic NKG2D upregulation on tumor-infiltrating NK cells in B16 tumors.
source: Blocking RAE-1ε but not RAE-1δ caused dramatic NKG2D upregulation on tumor-infiltrating NK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from tumor-infiltrating NK cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating NK cells in RAE-1-KO mice had elevated NKG2D compared with WT controls in B16 tumors.
source: Because B16 tumors completely lack expression of NKG2D ligands, we suspected an endogenous source of RAE-1ε, so we analyzed NK cells infiltrating B16 tumors implanted in WT or RAE-1-KO mice. Tumor-infiltrating NK cells mice had elevated NKG2D in RAE-1-KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from tumor-infiltrating NK cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Similar results were obtained when tumor-infiltrating NK cells were examined in mice implanted subcutaneously with syngeneic RMA-S lymphoma cells.
source: Similar results were obtained when tumor-infiltrating NK cells were examined in mice implanted subcutaneously with syngeneic RMA-S lymphoma cells, which also completely lack NKG2D ligand expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from tumor-infiltrating NK cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RMA-S lymphoma cells completely lack NKG2D ligand expression.
source: Similar results were obtained when tumor-infiltrating NK cells were examined in mice implanted subcutaneously with syngeneic RMA-S lymphoma cells, which also completely lack NKG2D ligand expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of RMA-S cells.

claim: Nonhematopoietic RAE-1ε was dominant in downregulating NKG2D in B16 tumors.
source: We analyzed RAE-1 bone marrow chimeras to determine the cellular compartment of RAE-1ε in the tumor microenvironment. We found that nonhematopoietic RAE-1ε was dominant in downregulating NKG2D in B16 tumors (Figure 5C), although in some experiments hematopoietic RAE-1 molecules seemed to show some variable effect, albeit not statistically significant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimera experiments with tumors shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tumor-associated endothelial cells expressed copious RAE-1ε in B16, RMA-S, and TRAMP-C2 tumor models.
source: We analyzed single-cell suspensions from B16, RMA-S, and TRAMP-C2 (prostate adenocarcinoma model) and found that tumor-associated endothelial cells expressed copious RAE-1ε (Figure 5D) in all tumor models tested.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RAE-1ε expression on tumor-associated endothelial cells was much greater than on lymph node BECs.
source: When we quantified RAE-1ε levels on tumor-associated endothelial cells compared with lymph node BECs, we saw a much greater expression of RAE-1ε on tumor-associated ECs (Figure 5E), indicating that the tumor microenvironment is a substantial inducer of endothelial RAE-1ε.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The tumor microenvironment is a substantial inducer of endothelial RAE-1ε.
source: When we quantified RAE-1ε levels on tumor-associated endothelial cells compared with lymph node BECs, we saw a much greater expression of RAE-1ε on tumor-associated ECs (Figure 5E), indicating that the tumor microenvironment is a substantial inducer of endothelial RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tumor-associated endothelial cells have higher RAE-1ε than lymph node endothelial cells.

claim: Healthy leg muscle lacked endothelial RAE-1ε expression.
source: Established KP sarcomas or matched healthy tissue from the opposite leg were dissociated and analyzed for endothelial RAE-1ε. Healthy leg muscle lacked endothelial RAE-1ε expression, whereas endothelial cells in KP sarcomas showed robust RAE-1ε induction (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Endothelial cells in KP sarcomas showed robust RAE-1ε induction.
source: Established KP sarcomas or matched healthy tissue from the opposite leg were dissociated and analyzed for endothelial RAE-1ε. Healthy leg muscle lacked endothelial RAE-1ε expression, whereas endothelial cells in KP sarcomas showed robust RAE-1ε induction (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating NK cells are engaged by non-tumor RAE-1ε.
source: Together, these data suggested that: (1) tumor-infiltrating NK cells are engaged by non-tumor RAE-1ε; (2) nonhematopoietic cells are the primary endogenous source of RAE-1ε responsible for NKG2D engagement; and (3) endothelial cells in transplanted tumors and autochthonous models of mouse cancer are induced to express especially high amounts of RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from tumor studies.

claim: Nonhematopoietic cells are the primary endogenous source of RAE-1ε responsible for NKG2D engagement in tumors.
source: Together, these data suggested that: (1) tumor-infiltrating NK cells are engaged by non-tumor RAE-1ε; (2) nonhematopoietic cells are the primary endogenous source of RAE-1ε responsible for NKG2D engagement; and (3) endothelial cells in transplanted tumors and autochthonous models of mouse cancer are induced to express especially high amounts of RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from tumor studies.

claim: Endothelial cells in transplanted tumors and autochthonous models of mouse cancer are induced to express especially high amounts of RAE-1ε.
source: Together, these data suggested that: (1) tumor-infiltrating NK cells are engaged by non-tumor RAE-1ε; (2) nonhematopoietic cells are the primary endogenous source of RAE-1ε responsible for NKG2D engagement; and (3) endothelial cells in transplanted tumors and autochthonous models of mouse cancer are induced to express especially high amounts of RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from tumor studies.

claim: NK cells recruited to tumors are engaged by RAE-1ε induced on endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which NK cells recruited to tumors are engaged by RAE-1ε induced on endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: NKG2D-KO mice showed reduced and delayed mortality compared with matched WT controls when challenged with B16 cells intravenously.
source: WT and NKG2D-KO mice were injected intravenously with a limiting number of B16 cells and monitored for survival. Consistent with our hypothesis, NKG2D-KO mice showed reduced and delayed mortality compared with matched WT controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NK depletion resulted in dramatically accelerated mortality in WT and NKG2D-KO mice challenged with B16 cells, eliminating the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency.
source: Importantly, NK depletion resulted in dramatically accelerated mortality in WT and NKG2D-KO mice, eliminating the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency.
evidence: Supported by survival data from NK-depleted mice.

claim: NKG2D-KO mice were more capable of controlling B16 tumor growth than WT counterparts when implanted subcutaneously.
source: When WT or NKG2D-KO mice were implanted with B16 cells subcutaneously, NKG2D-KO mice were more capable of controlling B16 tumor growth than WT counterparts (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice.
source: We also found that Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice, indicating that T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency against B16 tumors.
source: We also found that Rag2/NKG2D double knockout mice resisted B16 tumors better than Rag2-KO mice, indicating that T cells (and B cells) are not required for the protective effect of NKG2D deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the protective effect persists in Rag2-KO background.

claim: Treatment of NKG2D-WT mice with anti-NKG2D antibody in vivo starting the day before tumor cell implantation resulted in enhanced control of B16 tumors comparable to the NKG2D-KO mice.
source: A subsequent experiment on the Rag2-KO background showed that treatment of NKG2D-WT mice with anti-NKG2D antibody in vivo starting the day before tumor cell implantation resulted in enhanced control of B16 tumors comparable to the NKG2D-KO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NKG2D-KO mice showed better control of subcutaneous RMA-S tumors than did their WT counterparts.
source: We then turned to the RMA-S lymphoma transplant tumor model, which is targeted in vivo by NK cells through 'missing self' recognition but also does not express NKG2D ligands. NKG2D-KO mice showed better control of subcutaneous RMA-S tumors than did their WT counterparts (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands.
source: These data indicate that NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands, and that this desensitizing effect is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claim: The desensitizing effect of NKG2D is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
source: These data indicate that NKG2D expression mitigates in vivo NK responses to tumors that lack NKG2D ligands, and that this desensitizing effect is reversed by acute antibody blockade of NKG2D.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments with antibody blockade.

claim: The growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: Despite the NK hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-deficient animals, NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1, and the growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1.
source: Despite the NK hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-deficient animals, NKG2D-KO NK cells cannot recognize MULT1, and the growth of B16-MULT1 tumors was accelerated in NKG2D-KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NKG2D-KO NK cells.

claim: NKG2D interactions with tumor NKG2D ligands have a strong protective role.
source: These data are consistent with previous studies showing a strong protective role for NKG2D interactions with tumor NKG2D ligands (Cerwenka et al., 2001; Diefenbach et al., 2001; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RAE-1-KO mice challenged with B16-MULT1 tumors exhibited superior tumor rejection compared with WT mice.
source: Indeed, RAE-1-KO mice challenged with B16-MULT1 tumors exhibited superior tumor rejection compared with WT mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells.
source: We then turned to a transplant tumor model with endogenous NKG2D ligand expression, the TRAMP-C2 model of prostate adenocarcinoma. TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells, and this sensitivity is partly dependent on NKG2D (Jamieson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: TRAMP-C2 cell sensitivity to NK cells is partly dependent on NKG2D.
source: We then turned to a transplant tumor model with endogenous NKG2D ligand expression, the TRAMP-C2 model of prostate adenocarcinoma. TRAMP-C2 cells express RAE-1δ and RAE-1ε and are sensitive to NK cells, and this sensitivity is partly dependent on NKG2D (Jamieson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAE-1-KO mice showed enhanced control of TRAMP-C2 tumors compared with WT controls.
source: When injected subcutaneously into WT and RAE-1-KO mice, the RAE-1-KO mice showed enhanced control of TRAMP-C2 tumors compared with WT controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo, whereas NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claim: NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that interactions between NKG2D and endogenous RAE-1ε desensitize NK responses to tumors in vivo, whereas NKG2D ligands expressed on tumor cells promote antitumor NK responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the tumor challenge experiments.

claim: NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface.
source: We show that the activating receptor NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface, and leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: NKG2D engagement by endogenous RAE-1ε leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
source: We show that the activating receptor NKG2D is engaged by endogenous RAE-1ε in healthy WT mice, causing constitutive downregulation of NKG2D from the NK cell surface, and leads to an intrinsic global desensitization of NK cells to acute stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Preventing NKG2D interactions with host RAE-1ε enhanced NK cell antitumor responses in vivo.
source: Moreover, preventing NKG2D interactions with host RAE-1ε enhanced NK cell antitumor responses in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Endothelial cells were found to express RAE-1ε constitutively in lymph nodes.
source: Bone marrow chimera experiments identified nonhematopoietic cells as the dominant source of RAE-1ε, and endothelial cells were found to express RAE-1ε constitutively in lymph nodes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: RAE-1ε expression on tumor-associated endothelial cells was super-induced compared to endothelial cells in lymph nodes.
source: In tumors, RAE-1ε expression on tumor-associated endothelial cells was super-induced compared to endothelial cells in lymph nodes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Endothelial RAE-1ε interacts with NKG2D to desensitize NK cells and diminish antitumor NK responses.
source: These data support a model in which endothelial RAE-1ε interacts with NKG2D to desensitize NK cells and diminish antitumor NK responses.
evidence: This is a summary model based on the experimental findings.

claim: NK cell hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice has been reported previously by several groups.
source: NK cell hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice has been reported previously by several groups including ours (Zafirova et al., 2009; Sheppard et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015), although the trend of increased responsiveness did not reach statistical significance in our original characterization of the NKG2D-KO mouse (Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The trend of increased responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice did not reach statistical significance in the original characterization of the NKG2D-KO mouse.
source: NK cell hyper-responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice has been reported previously by several groups including ours (Zafirova et al., 2009; Sheppard et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015), although the trend of increased responsiveness did not reach statistical significance in our original characterization of the NKG2D-KO mouse (Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D can participate in immune surveillance of cancer by recognizing NKG2D ligands on tumor cells to induce NK cell activation and tumor cell killing.
source: At the same time, our results support the classical view that NKG2D can participate in immune surveillance of cancer by recognizing NKG2D ligands on tumor cells to induce NK cell activation and tumor cell killing (Diefenbach et al., 2000; Cerwenka et al., 2001; Diefenbach et al., 2001; Jamieson et al., 2002; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2D confers opposing effects, both promoting killing of tumor cells that express NKG2D ligands, and desensitizing NK cells through interactions with host ligands.
source: Hence, NKG2D confers opposing effects, both promoting killing of tumor cells that express NKG2D ligands, and desensitizing NK cells through interactions with host ligands.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The net outcome of NKG2D's opposing effects depends on the complement of NK-activating ligands that a given tumor cell expresses, among other factors.
source: We propose that the net outcome of these opposing effects of NKG2D depends on the complement of NK-activating ligands that a given tumor cell expresses, among other factors.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: For tumor cells that express abundant NKG2D ligands, the ability of NKG2D to promote acute activation against the tumor can outweigh the opposing desensitizing interactions with host cells.
source: For tumor cells that express abundant NKG2D ligands, the ability of NKG2D to promote acute activation against the tumor can outweigh the opposing desensitizing interactions with host cells.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Loss of NKG2D results in reduced tumor killing of B16-MULT1 tumors and YAC-1 cells.
source: In this circumstance, loss of NKG2D results in reduced tumor killing, as exemplified by the observation that NKG2D-deficient mice show reduced killing/rejection of B16-MULT1 tumors and YAC-1 cells (Figure 6D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Jamieson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2D-KO mice were defective in immune surveillance of spontaneous tumors that express NKG2D ligands, such as prostate adenocarcinomas in TRAMP mice and lymphomas in Eu-Myc mice.
source: We speculate that this situation also applies to previous findings that NKG2D-KO mice were defective in immune surveillance of spontaneous tumors that express NKG2D ligands, such as prostate adenocarcinomas in TRAMP mice and lymphomas in Eu-Myc mice (Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on previous findings cited from published literature.

claim: For tumor cells that express abundant other NK-activating ligands and either do not express NKG2D ligands or depend little on NKG2D ligands for NK killing, the global desensitization of NK cells caused by NKG2D interactions with host ligands is predicted to exert a dominant effect.
source: In contrast, for tumor cells that express abundant other NK-activating ligands, and either do not express NKG2D ligands (e.g. RMA-S and B16 cells), or depend little on NKG2D ligands for NK killing, the global desensitization of NK cells caused by NKG2D interactions with host ligands is predicted to exert a dominant effect.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: In a spontaneous model of hepatocellular carcinoma, NKG2D-KO mice exhibited a reduced tumor incidence.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that in a spontaneous model of hepatocellular carcinoma, NKG2D-KO mice exhibited a reduced tumor incidence (Sheppard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NKG2D-mediated desensitization may be dominant in the hepatocellular carcinoma model.
source: We speculate that NKG2D-mediated desensitization may be dominant in that model, though the authors offered an alternative explanation for their findings.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of published findings.

claim: Some tumor environments may contain signals that reverse NKG2D-mediated desensitization while preserving NKG2D-mediated activation, or vice versa.
source: It is also possible that some tumor environments contain signals that reverse NKG2D-mediated desensitization while preserving NKG2D-mediated activation, or vice versa.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The net effect of NKG2D will likely depend on the activating and inhibitory ligands tumor cells express, as well as the context of the tumor microenvironment.
source: Thus, the net effect of NKG2D will likely depend on the activating and inhibitory ligands tumor cells express, as well as the context of the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Endogenous RAE-1ε played a significant role in NK desensitization, but it does not completely account for the desensitizing activity of NKG2D.
source: Although endogenous RAE-1ε played a significant role in NK desensitization, it does not completely account for the desensitizing activity of NKG2D, based on the finding that NK cells attained higher responsiveness in NKG2D-KO mice than in RAE-1-KO mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Endogenous interactions of NKG2D with RAE-1ε cause steady-state NK cell desensitization.
source: While our data clearly support a model in which endogenous interactions of NKG2D with RAE-1ε cause steady-state NK cell desensitization, we do not rule out other potential mechanisms contributing to hyper-responsiveness of NKG2D-KO cells -- such as interactions of NKG2D with other ligands at steady state, or 'tonic' signaling through NKG2D, at steady state or during NK development.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the data and possible alternative mechanisms.

claim: Other potential mechanisms may contribute to hyper-responsiveness of NKG2D-KO cells, such as interactions of NKG2D with other ligands at steady state, or 'tonic' signaling through NKG2D.
source: While our data clearly support a model in which endogenous interactions of NKG2D with RAE-1ε cause steady-state NK cell desensitization, we do not rule out other potential mechanisms contributing to hyper-responsiveness of NKG2D-KO cells -- such as interactions of NKG2D with other ligands at steady state, or 'tonic' signaling through NKG2D, at steady state or during NK development.
evidence: This is speculation about possible alternative mechanisms.

claim: NKG2D ligand expression in adult mice has been thought largely restricted to cells undergoing certain stress responses associated with oncogenesis or infection.
source: Perhaps the most surprising finding in this report is the expression and functional relevance of RAE-1ε on endothelial cells. NKG2D ligand expression in adult mice has been thought largely restricted to cells undergoing certain stress responses associated with oncogenesis or infection, but here we show that blood endothelial cells and lymphoid endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid organs of healthy animals express RAE-1ε at steady-state.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field.

claim: Blood endothelial cells and lymphoid endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid organs of healthy animals express RAE-1ε at steady-state.
source: Perhaps the most surprising finding in this report is the expression and functional relevance of RAE-1ε on endothelial cells. NKG2D ligand expression in adult mice has been thought largely restricted to cells undergoing certain stress responses associated with oncogenesis or infection, but here we show that blood endothelial cells and lymphoid endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid organs of healthy animals express RAE-1ε at steady-state.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Endothelium in several tissues was completely negative for RAE-1ε in the same mice where lymph node endothelium expressed RAE-1ε.
source: It was striking that, in the same mice, endothelium in several other tissues was completely negative for RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The lymphoid tissue environment imparts specific signals that upregulate RAE-1ε on associated endothelial cells.
source: These findings suggest that the lymphoid tissue environment imparts specific signals that upregulate RAE-1ε on associated endothelial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RAE-1ε is expressed on lymph node endothelium but not on endothelium in other tissues.

claim: Specific expression of RAE-1ε on endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid tissue suggests that the system may be designed to desensitize NK cells that traverse this tissue.
source: Specific expression on endothelial cells in secondary lymphoid tissue further suggests that the system may be designed to desensitize NK cells that traverse this tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Non-hematopoietic cells are the dominant source of RAE-1ε-mediated NK desensitization.
source: It is important to note that our data clearly identify non-hematopoietic cells as the dominant source of RAE-1ε-mediated NK desensitization, but we cannot conclusively establish endothelial cells as relevant desensitizing compartment without an endothelial-specific RAE-1ε-KO mouse.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings and acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: Endothelial cells cannot be conclusively established as the relevant desensitizing compartment without an endothelial-specific RAE-1ε-KO mouse.
source: It is important to note that our data clearly identify non-hematopoietic cells as the dominant source of RAE-1ε-mediated NK desensitization, but we cannot conclusively establish endothelial cells as relevant desensitizing compartment without an endothelial-specific RAE-1ε-KO mouse.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: Resident liver NK cells (CD49a-neg CD49b+) were engaged by host RAE-1ε.
source: We were also surprised to find that resident liver NK cells (CD49a-neg CD49b+) were engaged by host RAE-1ε.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Little to no RAE-1ε was detected in cell suspensions from liver.
source: We do not know the cellular source of RAE-1ε responsible for engaging these NK cells, as we detected little to no RAE-1ε in cell suspensions from liver.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Resident liver NK cells might traffic to distinct anatomical structures, perhaps liver-specific lymphoid tissue, that might contain RAE-1ε-expressing cells.
source: We speculate that resident liver NK cells might traffic to distinct anatomical structures, perhaps liver-specific lymphoid tissue, that might contain RAE-1ε-expressing cells.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: RAE-1ε was expressed on vasculature in all tumor models tested, including transplant models of melanoma, lymphoma, prostate cancer, and the genetically engineered KP model of autochthonous sarcoma.
source: We found especially high levels of RAE-1ε on endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment. Notably, RAE-1ε was expressed on vasculature in all tumor models tested, including transplant models of melanoma, lymphoma, prostate cancer, and the genetically engineered KP model of autochthonous sarcoma.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Levels of tumor-associated endothelial RAE-1ε were even greater than on endothelial cells in draining and non-draining lymph nodes.
source: In all cases, levels of tumor-associated endothelial RAE-1ε were even greater than on endothelial cells in draining and non-draining lymph nodes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: RAE-1 expression has been linked to high levels of cellular proliferation in development and wound healing.
source: Vasculature in the tumor microenvironment is extremely dynamic, characterized by extensive angiogenesis. RAE-1 expression has been linked to high levels of cellular proliferation in development and wound healing (Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A similar mechanism to that linking RAE-1 expression to cellular proliferation may be responsible for the super-induced expression of RAE-1ε on neovasculature in tumors.
source: Perhaps a similar mechanism is responsible for the super-induced expression of RAE-1ε on neovasculature in tumors.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Endothelial cells have been shown to produce immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: Endothelial cells are sometimes thought of as passive circulatory conduits. Our data and other studies clearly paint a more complex picture. Endothelial cells have recently been shown to produce immunomodulatory cytokines, and lymph node endothelial cells can tolerize peripheral T cells by presenting self MHC – peptide complexes (Rouhani et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Lymph node endothelial cells can tolerize peripheral T cells by presenting self MHC – peptide complexes.
source: Endothelial cells are sometimes thought of as passive circulatory conduits. Our data and other studies clearly paint a more complex picture. Endothelial cells have recently been shown to produce immunomodulatory cytokines, and lymph node endothelial cells can tolerize peripheral T cells by presenting self MHC – peptide complexes (Rouhani et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Endothelial cells regulate NK cell activity.
source: The data in our study add to the emerging role of endothelial cells as active regulators in the immune response by suggesting that endothelial cells regulate NK cell activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple NK cell receptors are known to regulate NK cell responsiveness.
source: Because multiple NK cell receptors are known to regulate NK cell responsiveness, we are intrigued by the possibility that endothelial cells may also regulate NK cell activity through other receptor-ligand systems.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Endothelial cells may regulate NK cell activity through other receptor-ligand systems besides NKG2D-RAE-1ε.
source: Because multiple NK cell receptors are known to regulate NK cell responsiveness, we are intrigued by the possibility that endothelial cells may also regulate NK cell activity through other receptor-ligand systems.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: NK cells may have effects on endothelial cell biology, through NKG2D-RAE-1ε or other mechanisms.
